text: Microsoft's own guidance here is genuinely explicit: migration doesn't have to mean rebuilding everything by hand. Mounting your existing ADF as a native Fabric item gives you visibility and side-by-side testing with zero pipeline rework. The built-in upgrade experience assesses each pipeline as Ready, Needs review, Coming soon, or Not compatible. And manual migration handles the complex, low-parity cases the other two paths genuinely can't.

Three real paths, chosen by how much your pipelines actually differ from what Fabric supports natively — start by mounting, lean on the upgrade tool where you can, and reserve manual rebuilding for the genuinely complex cases.
In ADF, a dataset is its own reusable object — file path and format settings configured once, referenced by many activities across your pipelines.

In Fabric, that same information moves inline, directly into the Copy activity's own Source tab. When you migrate manually, this is genuinely the single most common, repetitive task: every ADF dataset your pipelines reference becomes inline configuration on whichever activity actually used it.

A real, honest list worth knowing before you promise a stakeholder a timeline. Azure-SSIS integration runtime is genuinely still to be determined in Fabric — if your pipelines run real SSIS packages, plan to keep them on classic ADF for now. The Validation activity has no direct equivalent either, but rebuilds cleanly with Get Metadata and If Condition together. And five separate HDInsight activities collapse into just one unified activity type in Fabric.

Three real paths, a concrete dataset-to-inline pattern, and an honest list of what still needs manual rework. Next: When to Choose ADF vs. Fabric — putting this entire comparison together and making the real call for a genuine project.
